clue.text: It's undisguised anger, by gum!

parts.note: undisguised means open and candid, i.e. frank
to incense is to anger

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in open, honest fury: 'By gum!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'By gum!' reads as a mild northern English oath, but 'gum' is the definition and 'by' only joins it.
explanation.definitionFit: This aromatic resin from Boswellia trees is a classic gum, burnt as incense.

clue.text: Season for goodwill takes in start of Lent

indicators.note: the word for goodwill takes in, i.e. contains, the next piece

parts.note: favour is goodwill or kindly regard

indicators.note: start of picks only the opening letter of the word Lent

explanation.surface: The season of goodwill somehow welcomes the beginning of Lent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Season' looks like a noun (Christmas, the season of goodwill) but is the verb, to add taste.
explanation.definitionFit: To season food is to give it taste, which is what this verb means.

clue.text: Alternative nominations replacing Elias as an example

indicators.note: replacing here means putting the letters back in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Other names are proposed to stand in for someone called Elias, by way of illustration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'an example' only rounds off the surface: the letters of ELIAS and AS are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Assumed names are other names a person goes by, so they are alternative nominations in a playful sense.

clue.text: Supporters in the house for the Royal Mail?

explanation.definitionFit: Roof timbers rising from tie beam to ridge hold up a house; a monarch's letters would jokingly be a monarch's own post.

clue.text: No sound from the horse's mouth

definitions.text: No sound from the horse's mouth

parts.words: No sound from the horse's mouth
parts.note: a horse's call is said exactly like the old word 'nay' for No, so 'No' sounds like what comes from the horse's mouth

explanation.surface: Not a whisper of information comes straight from the source.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From the horse's mouth' is the idiom for first-hand information, but here it is literal: the noise a horse makes, which sounds like 'nay'.
explanation.definitionFit: The cry a horse gives is the familiar whinny it utters.

clue.text: Account for the old harbour board's Northern Ireland turnover

parts.note: ex- means former, old
the PLA is the Port of London Authority, which runs the Thames harbour

indicators.note: turnover means the abbreviation for Northern Ireland is turned round

explanation.surface: An auditor must justify the former port authority's Ulster revenue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turnover' looks like business revenue but signals reversal. The PLA (Port of London Authority) runs London's river port.
explanation.definitionFit: To give the reasons for something is to make it clear, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Heart-throb crept away from steam yacht

parts.note: SY is the abbreviation for steam yacht, as in SY Morning
stole, past tense of steal, means crept away quietly

explanation.surface: A romantic idol sneaked off a steamer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart-throb' suggests a matinee idol but means one beat of the heart.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the contraction phase of the heartbeat, a single throb of the heart.

clue.text: Bad language produced by ranking followed by stage-management

parts.note: billing is an actor's ranking on a poster (top billing)

indicators.note: management suggests the letters of stage being handled and rearranged

explanation.surface: Theatre folk swear over who gets top billing and how the stage is run.
explanation.walkthrough: BILLINGSGATE was London's fish market, its porters famous for foul language. 'management' turns STAGE into SGATE.
explanation.definitionFit: The fish market's porters gave their name to coarse abusive speech.

clue.text: Persian princess captured by Scot

indicators.note: captured by means held inside the next-named word

parts.note: Ian is a typical Scottish name, so a Scot
a rani is an Indian princess or queen

explanation.surface: A Persian royal is kidnapped by a Scotsman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Persian' looks like an adjective for the princess but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Persia is the old name of Iran, so a Persian is a native of that country.

clue.text: Troublesome as MEP, is producing deadlock

indicators.note: troublesome suggests the letters are disordered and stirred up

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A difficult Euro MP is causing a stalemate.
explanation.definitionFit: A position from which no progress is possible is a stalemate, a deadlock.

clue.text: Accommodation offered by these (for instance) New York spies?

definitions.text: Accommodation offered by these (for instance) New York spies?

parts.words: Accommodation offered by these (for instance) New York spies?
parts.note: houses are offered for sale or rent by property firms; read again, New York is one of the US states, so its spies serve that state

explanation.surface: Spies from New York, for example, offer lodging.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading jokes that New York's secret agents, working for one of the fifty states, are in the property business.
explanation.definitionFit: These firms arrange the sale and letting of houses, so they offer homes to buyers and tenants.

clue.text: Improves appearance at the University

parts.note: looks means appearance
up means in residence at university, as in up at Oxford

explanation.surface: Someone's looks get better once at university.
explanation.walkthrough: To be UP is the British idiom for being in residence at a university.
explanation.definitionFit: When things get better we say they are on the rise, an idiom for improving.

clue.text: Governor with an old party is not to cut short the audience

definitions.text: not to cut short the audience

parts.note: HE, His Excellency, is the title of a governor
an gives the article A
rout is an old word for a large evening party

explanation.surface: A governor with an outdated political party refuses to curtail the hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'party' looks political, but a rout was a fashionable gathering in Georgian times.
explanation.definitionFit: To listen to someone until they have finished is to let them have their full say.

clue.text: On the stage: Owen takes breathers

explanation.definitionFit: Owen Nares was a British stage and screen matinee idol; the word is also the anatomical name for nostrils, through which we breathe.

clue.text: Tight cord with ten parts twisted

parts.note: string is cord

indicators.note: the word ten is pulled apart and twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: A taut cord is made of ten strands twisted together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'parts twisted' rearranges TEN into ENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Strict, rigorous rules are tight ones, a close synonym.

clue.text: He follows the form-book religiously

parts.note: a form-book suggests horse racing form, but here the forms are the set words of a church service, observed devoutly

explanation.surface: A punter sticks rigidly to the racing form guide.
explanation.walkthrough: The form-book is a racing guide in the surface; in the second reading it is a book of liturgical forms, and 'religiously' is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone devoted to fixed ceremonial forms in worship is a stickler for liturgy.

clue.text: A spell of gymnastic exercise for county team, say

indicators.note: say means the county name is spoken and heard as another word

parts.note: Somerset is an English county with a cricket team

explanation.surface: A gymnastics session to help the county side.
explanation.walkthrough: SOMERSET is a county in south-west England; SUMMERSET is an old spelling of somersault.
explanation.definitionFit: An old form of 'somersault', a tumbling head-over-heels flip in gymnastics.

clue.text: Feel lack of a heater, perhaps? Don't go off!

definitions.text: Feel lack of a heater, perhaps?

explanation.definitionFit: Missing a fire is jokingly what the word says; a gun that fails to discharge does this.

clue.text: Learned rite due for revision

indicators.note: for revision means the letters are to be revised into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone has studied a ceremony that needs updating.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan prints 'rite', misread as 'rile'; RITE plus DUE rearranged give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A scholarly person is well read, so learned is a direct synonym.

clue.text: A slab of this sort would, we hear, float

definitions.text: A slab of this sort would, we hear, float

indicators.note: of this sort hints at sorting the letters of A slab into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is told that a slab of a certain material would float.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines a very light wood famous for floating, and 'sort' rearranges A SLAB.
explanation.definitionFit: This feather-light tropical timber is used for rafts and models because it floats.

clue.text: Cash that's needed for the club

parts.note: brass is slang for money
i.e. stands for id est, that is

explanation.surface: Money is required to join the club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'club' looks like a society with a fee; it is an old golf club, a number two wood.
explanation.definitionFit: An old wooden golf club with a brass sole plate.

clue.text: Watchman's prospect in his own affair

explanation.definitionFit: A sentry is a lookout; a view or outlook is a prospect; and 'that's his lookout' means his own concern.

clue.text: Attack a sailor in speech

indicators.note: in speech means the phrase is heard spoken, sounding like another word

parts.note: a salt is an old sailor

explanation.surface: Someone verbally lays into a seaman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in speech' looks like a verbal attack, but it signals the sound of A SALT.
explanation.definitionFit: An assault is a violent onslaught, a synonym for attack.

clue.text: Doctrine that may be taken both ways

indicators.text: that may be taken both ways
indicators.note: taken both ways means the letters read the same forwards and backwards

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A belief that can be interpreted in two senses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken both ways' sounds like ambiguity but means reading in either direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A principle held as true by a group is a doctrine.

clue.text: "See 'ere" said Jack on his own

parts.note: a jack (jack tar) is a sailor, abbreviated AB, able seaman
alone means on his own

explanation.surface: Jack, by himself, says 'See here!' in a Cockney accent.
explanation.walkthrough: The shellfish is also called a sea-ear, which "See 'ere" said aloud sounds like.
explanation.definitionFit: This edible shellfish is known as a sea-ear (ormer) for its ear-shaped shell.

clue.text: Impression produced by bookmaker?

explanation.walkthrough: 'bookmaker' wants to be a racing bookie; read literally, it is a publisher.
explanation.definitionFit: A print run of a book is an impression; and a bookmaker, read as a maker of books, publishes one.

clue.text: Briefly popular drink

parts.note: in means fashionable, popular
a short is a small measure of spirits

explanation.surface: A quick, well-liked tot.
explanation.walkthrough: A SHORT is British pub slang for a measure of spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: To say something concisely is to put it in a few words, a phrase meaning briefly.

clue.text: The way Nash planned Prinny's party, so it's said

indicators.note: so it's said means the phrase is spoken and heard as another

parts.note: Prinny was the nickname of the Prince Regent, later George IV, so his party is the Regent's treat

explanation.surface: Nash designed the Prince Regent's celebration, according to rumour.
explanation.walkthrough: John Nash laid out this London thoroughfare for the Prince Regent (Prinny); 'way' is a road.
explanation.definitionFit: This road is the London thoroughfare the architect John Nash designed for the Regent.
